::: {.callout-note title="Learning outcomes & Chapter summary"}

1. **Explain** how a density plot represents the concentration of observations without dividing them into bins.

2. **Adjust** the bandwidth and **evaluate** which features of a distribution remain visible at different amounts of smoothing.

3. **Compare** multiple distributions using overlapping density curves and facets with common scales.

4. **Combine** density plots with individual observations and medians, and **interpret** violin plots as mirrored densities.

:::

## Why bother?

In [Distributions](9_distributions.qmd),
we used histograms to see patterns that were hidden by overlapping observations.
But the appearance of a histogram depends on the width and placement of its bins.
And when we want to compare several groups in one chart,
overlapping bars can make their shapes difficult to follow.

::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

In the previous chapter,
we learned that
since histograms start with binning the axis
and then count the observation within each bin equally
no matter how close to the edge of the bin they are.
This gave rise to one of the shortcomings of histograms:
that the exact position of the bins along the axis
could drastically impact the appearance of the histogram
and lead to varying perceptions of the underlying distribution
as we saw in @fig-hist-bin-shift.

Can you try to think of how we could change
the histogram creation process
to remedy this shortcoming?
Study the animation schematic in @fig-hist-buildup again
to help you brainstorm possible improvements.

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

Maybe we could take a more **observation-centric** approach
for the bin placement?

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

Instead of first binning the axis,
we could center each bin on its observation.
Where nearby bins overlap,
their heights (i.e. the counts) will be added together,
but only for the overlapping part,
as can be seen in this animation:

![Animated schematic of centering each bin on the observation](img/kde-rectangle-kernel-buildup.gif){#fig-kde-rect-buildup}

This modification removes the need to select
fixed intervals for the bins along the axis,
and thus makes the appearance of the distribution
only depend on the width of each bin
(i.e. one parameter less than the histogram.

If we applied this technique to the data used in @fig-hist-bin-shift,
we would always end up with the following chart
since the position of the bins is centered on each observation.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-hist-bin-shift-ch10
#| fig-cap: Centering the bins on each observation creates histogram-like chart chart that does not depend on bin placement.
from random import choice
import altair as alt

cars = alt.datasets.data.cars()
bin_min = 235
bin_max = 285

mask_to_replace = cars['Displacement'].between(bin_min, bin_max)
new_values = [choice(range(bin_max, 300)) for _ in range(mask_to_replace.sum())]
cars.loc[mask_to_replace, 'Displacement'] = new_values

# hist = alt.Chart(cars, height=120, width=200).mark_bar().encode(
#     alt.X('Displacement').bin().title(None).scale(domain=(20, 500)),
#     alt.Y('count()').title(None)
# )
# tick_values = values=list(range(0, 500, 50))
# hist | hist.encode(
#     alt.X('Displacement')
#     .bin(nice=False, extent=[35, 490])
#     .title(None)
#     .scale(domain=(20, 500))
#     .axis(
#         labelExpr=(
#             f"indexof({tick_values}, datum.value - 35) % 2 === 0"
#             " ? datum.label : ''"
#         ),
#     ),
# )


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.neighbors import KernelDensity

values = cars["Displacement"].dropna().to_numpy()

# Half-width of each rectangular kernel, in your variable's units
bandwidth = 50

kde = KernelDensity(
    kernel="tophat",
    bandwidth=bandwidth,
).fit(values.reshape(-1, 1))

# Evaluate the estimated density on a fine grid
x = np.linspace(
    values.min(), #- 2 * bandwidth,
    values.max(), #+ 2 * bandwidth,
    25,
)

density = pd.DataFrame({
    "value": x,
    "density": np.exp(kde.score_samples(x.reshape(-1, 1))),
})

n = len(values)  # Observations used to fit the KDE
bin_width = 50    # Match your histogram's bin width
density["Count"] = density["density"] * n * bin_width

bars = density.sort_values("value").copy()
bars["value_end"] = bars["value"].shift(-1)
bars = bars.dropna(subset=["value_end"])

alt.Chart(bars, height=120, width=200).mark_bar(
    binSpacing=0,
).encode(
    x=alt.X(
        "value:Q",
        bin="binned",
        title="Value",
        # scale=alt.Scale(domain=(20, 500)),
        # axis=alt.Axis(values=list(range(0, 500, 100)))
    ),
    x2="value_end:Q",
    y=alt.Y("Count"),
)

```

## Visualizing distributions with density plots

In the exercise,
we saw how centering the bin
on the observation
can lead to a more robust distribution plot.
Since we are no longer binning the axis
at fixed intervals,
this chart is technically no longer a histogram.
Rather,
it's called a density chart
since it is depicting
how the density of observations varies throughout the distribution.
The method we use to create a density chart
in the animation above
is called a "Kernel Density Estimation",
or "KDE" for short.
As the name implies,
this method is estimating
the unknown probability density function
(i.e. the density of the underlying *population*),
using kernels.

The "kernel" can be taught of as a bin
that is centered on the data point.
In the exercise above,
we used a rectangular kernel
to make the connection to histograms clearer.
An issue with this shape is that it contributes
a fully to the entire area within the kernel width
and then drastically falls off to zero outside.
Using a smoother kernel shape
has the advantage
of gradually reducing contribution from an observation
avoiding the sudden cutoff of a rectangular kernel.
The most commonly used shape is the Gaussian bell-shaped kernel,
and summing such smooth individual kernels together
would also produce a smooth density estimate for the entire distribution,
as we can see in @fig-density-buildup.

![Animated schematic of building a density estimate from individual observations using the typical bell-shaped kernels.](img/kde-buildup.gif){#fig-density-buildup}

<!-- TODO ref origin of gif -->

Let's create a density plot for the entire movie dataset,
before breaking it down into genres.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

In Altair,
we first calculate the density with `transform_density`,
then draw the resulting curve with a line or area mark.
The `as_` argument names the two output columns:
`Running Time min` contains positions along the x-axis,
and `Density` contains the estimated density at each position.
We also specify `:Q` for the new `Density` column
because it is calculated by the transform,
rather than being a column
whose type Altair can read from the original dataframe.

```{python}
#| label: runtime-kde-alt
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

alt.data_transformers.enable('vegafusion');
movies = pd.read_csv('data/movies.csv')

alt.Chart(movies, height=200).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    as_=['Running Time min', 'Density'],
).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min'),
    y=alt.Y('Density:Q'),
)
```

### ggplot

In ggplot, `geom_density()` both estimates the density
and draws its outline as a line.
We can fill the area under the curve by specifying `fill = 'grey'`
directly in the `geom`.

```{r}
#| label: runtime-kde-gg
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)

movies <- readr::read_csv('data/movies.csv')
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_density(fill = 'grey')
```

:::

As you can see above,
the y-axis is not showing the count of movies,
but rather their probability *density*,
which means the probability per unit of the x-axis.
A higher curve indicates a greater concentration of observations
around that runtime.

Importantly,
it is the area over an interval
(rather than the height at a specific point),
that represents an estimated proportion of observations
and the area of the entire density is normalized to sum to one
(i.e. 100% of the sample).
This means that the values on the y-axis
depends on the range of the values on the x-axis,
which can make the y-axis confusing to interpret
(as you will experience in the example with counts below).

For these reasons,
use densities primarily to understand the shape of a distribution,
rather than trying to read specific probabilities of the y-axis.
And although densities are generally well-perceived
also by non-technical audiences,
an advantage of histograms
is that they are simpler to interpret and explain.

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid using densities with counts

We can convert the density to a count
by multiplying the density values
with the total number of observations.
While this can be useful
to indicate how many observations there are,
it is not as straightforward to interpret
as the counts in a histogram.
Since the overall density *area*
would sum to the total number of observations in the sample,
a larger range on the x-axis
leads to lower counts on the y-axis as we can see in @fig-runtime-kde-count-alt.
Since the estimated density is continuous
rather than the step-shaped histogram outline,
what we see on the y-axis is really partial estimated counts.
While these peculiarities might make sense
when you understand how a density chart works
they are not intuitive and can lead to misinterpretations.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-runtime-kde-count-alt
#| fig-cap: Twice the range on the x-axis leads to half the counts on the y-axis while the shape of the distribution stays the same. This is because we are effectively having twice as many 1-unit intervals along the x-axis in the rightmost chart, so the count for each of those intervals must be half that of the original wider intervals in the leftmost chart.
density = alt.Chart(movies, height=120, width=220).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    as_=['Running Time min', 'Density'],
    counts=True
).mark_area(color="#FF0039").encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min:Q'),
    y=alt.Y('Density:Q').title('Estimated counts'),
)

density | alt.Chart(movies.assign(runtime_10 = lambda df: df['Running Time min'] * 2), height=120, width=220).transform_density(
    'runtime_10',
    as_=['2x Running Time min', 'Density'],
    counts=True
).mark_area(color="#FF0039").encode(
    x=alt.X('2x Running Time min:Q'),
    y=alt.Y('Density:Q').title('Estimated counts'),
)
```

:::

## Bandwidth

::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

Analogous to how we can set the width of each bin in a histogram,
we can also control how wide each kernel should be
via its bandwidth.
For the bell-shaped kernel,
the bandwidth equals its standard deviation.
What do you think happens to the shape of the density curve
when we make the bandwidth larger?

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

You can try a few different bandwidths 
on the marathon example from the previous chapter.
Can you see the same features as with the histograms?

```{python}
#| label: fig-marathon-density-bandwidth
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The same London Marathon finish times shown with different bandwidths.
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde

mara = pd.read_csv('data/london_marathon_finish_times.csv')
finish_times = mara['Time (minutes)'].to_numpy()
bandwidths = [0.5, 2, 5, 15]
grid = np.linspace(120, 540, 1681)

# Precompute this widget's curves so switching does not send all runners to the browser
# or repeat the density calculation there. gaussian_kde's factor is relative to the SD.
marathon_densities = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({
        'time': grid,
        'density': gaussian_kde(
            finish_times, bw_method=bandwidth / finish_times.std(ddof=1)
        )(grid),
        'bandwidth': bandwidth,
    })
    for bandwidth in bandwidths
], ignore_index=True)

bandwidth_param = alt.param(
    name='marathon_bandwidth',
    value=2,
    bind=alt.binding_select(options=bandwidths, name='Bandwidth (minutes): '),
)

alt.Chart(marathon_densities, height=200, width=500).transform_filter(
    alt.datum.bandwidth == bandwidth_param
).mark_area(opacity=0.6).encode(
    x=alt.X('time:Q').title('Finish time (minutes)').scale(domain=[120, 540]),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q').title('Density').scale(
        domain=[0, float(marathon_densities['density'].max()) * 1.05]
    ),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip('time:Q').title('Finish time (min)').format('.1f'),
        alt.Tooltip('density:Q').title('Density').format('.4f'),
    ],
).add_params(bandwidth_param)
```

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

A small bandwidth produces a more detailed, wiggly curve
whereas a large bandwidth produces a smoother curve.

:::::
::::
:::

One of the advantages of a density over a histogram
is that the estimation of the underlying PDF
is less influenced by the kernel bandwidth
than histograms are by bin width.
It is also notably easier
to approximate an optimal kernel bandwidth
compared to an optimal bin width,
so the default rules for density bandwidth estimation
can be quite effective.

However,
as we just saw in the exercise
there is no single bandwidth that answers every question best.
A wider bandwidth
can help us describe the overall spread of a distribution,
but it can also hide details and multimodality.
A more narrow bandwidth while a smaller one is useful
for investigating concentrations near particular targets,
but can introduce a spiky appearance
that makes it harder to
see the overall shape of the distribution.

With all that in mind,
let's see how we can change the bandwidth
for our density charts.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

Set `bandwidth` in `transform_density`.
It is measured in the units of the variable being plotted,
so a bandwidth of 2 here means two minutes.

```{python}
#| label: runtime-kde-bandwidth-alt
alt.Chart(movies, height=200).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    as_=['runtime', 'density'],
    bandwidth=2,
).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)').scale(zero=False),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q').title('Density'),
)
```

If left unset,
the default bandwidth estimation
is not very sophisticated,
so it is particularly important to try different bandwidths.

### ggplot

Set `bw` in `geom_density`.
It is measured in the units of the variable,
so `bw = 2` uses a bandwidth of two minutes.

```{r}
#| label: runtime-kde-bandwidth-gg
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_density(bw = 2, fill = 'grey80') +
    labs(x = 'Running time (min)', y = 'Density')
```

If left unset,
the default bandwidth estimation
is not very sophisticated,
but it is possible to switch to the Sheather-Jones estimation rule
which is among the best in finding a suitable bandwidth
that describes the distribution well on average.
The Sheather-Jones rule is [one of the recommended
defaults](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/density.html)
although the differences are more noticeable for multimodal distributions.
Remember that testing different bandwidths
can still reveal different features of the chart.

```{r}
#| label: runtime-kde-bandwidth-isj-gg
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_density(bw = 'SJ', fill = 'grey80') +
    labs(x = 'Running time (min)', y = 'Density')
```


:::

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid extending density curves beyond the data range

Since each observation contributes to the overall density
with a kernel centered on the observation,
this could lead to the density curve
extending into ranges that does not make
sense for the measured variable.
Take the (fictional) data set below
about how much time students spend on their phone during lecture.
The KDE in the chart to the right,
makes it seem like some students
spend a negative amount of time on their phones,
although there are naturally no observations beyond 0 min.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-kde-beyond-range
#| fig-cap: A KDE can either stop at the data range (left) or go past it (right).
# Synthetic observations: 40 students in a 60-minute lecture.
df = pd.DataFrame({"minutes": [
    0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7,
    1.9, 2, 2.2, 2.5, 2.8, 3.2, 3.8, 4.5, 5.5, 6.5,
    8, 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 40, 
]})

bin_width = 3
bandwidth = 2.5
x_domain = [-10, 50]
observed_range = [float(df.minutes.min()), float(df.minutes.max())]

histogram = alt.Chart(df).mark_bar(
    color="#b8c0c8", opacity=0.65, binSpacing=0
).encode(
    x=alt.X("minutes:Q",
            bin=alt.Bin(step=bin_width, extent=[0, 50]),
            scale=alt.Scale(domain=x_domain, nice=False),
            axis=alt.Axis(values=list(range(-10, 51, 10))),
            title="Minutes of phone use during lecture"),
    y=alt.Y("count():Q", title="Students (per 3-minute bin)"),
)


def panel(extent):
    kde = (
        alt.Chart(df)
        .transform_density(
            "minutes", bandwidth=bandwidth, counts=True,
            extent=extent, steps=601, as_=["minutes", "density"]
        )
        # counts=True gives n * density; multiply by bin width
        # to put the KDE on the histogram's count scale.
        .transform_calculate(smoothed_count=f"datum.density * {bin_width}")
        .mark_area(color="#FF0039", opacity=0.2,
                   line={"color": "#FF0039", "strokeWidth": 2})
        .encode(
            x=alt.X("minutes:Q",
                    scale=alt.Scale(domain=x_domain, nice=False),
                    axis=alt.Axis(values=list(range(-10, 51, 10))),
                    title="Minutes of phone use during lecture"),
            y=alt.Y("smoothed_count:Q", title="Students (per 3-minute bin)"),
        )
    )
    return (histogram + kde).properties(
        width=260, height=160
    )

chart = (
    alt.hconcat(
        panel(observed_range),
        panel(x_domain),
    )
    .resolve_scale(x="shared", y="shared")
)

chart
```

:::

## Adding back individual observations

::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

The curve below was calculated from a set of movie runtimes.
Before opening the solution,
sketch what you think the individual observations
might look like along the x-axis:
use a small tick for each movie to create a **rug plot**.
Roughly how many ticks would you draw, and where would you place them?

```{python}
#| label: sparse-runtime-density-question
#| echo: false
runtime_values = movies['Running Time min'].dropna().sort_values().to_numpy()
# Deliberately choose five observations spread across the empirical distribution.
# These are the observations nearest the midpoints of five equal-sized groups.
sparse_indices = ((np.arange(5) + 0.5) * len(runtime_values) / 5).astype(int)
sparse_runtimes = runtime_values[sparse_indices]
sparse_grid = np.linspace(40, 260, 441)
sparse_bandwidth = 18

runtime_comparison = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({
        'runtime': sparse_grid,
        'density': gaussian_kde(
            values, bw_method=sparse_bandwidth / values.std(ddof=1)
        )(sparse_grid),
        'sample': label,
    })
    for label, values in [('Five movies', sparse_runtimes), ('All movies', runtime_values)]
], ignore_index=True)
runtime_density_limit = float(runtime_comparison['density'].max()) * 1.05

def runtime_comparison_curve(label, width=420, height=160):
    return alt.Chart(
        runtime_comparison[runtime_comparison['sample'] == label],
        width=width, height=height,
    ).mark_area(opacity=0.6).encode(
        x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)').scale(domain=[40, 260]),
        y=alt.Y('density:Q').title('Density').scale(domain=[0, runtime_density_limit]),
    )

runtime_comparison_curve('Five movies')
```

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

Remember that the area under the curve is normalized to one
regardless of the number of movies.
Does a smooth outline necessarily imply
that there are many underlying observations
or could a very different number of observations produce a similar curve?

::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

There are only **five movies** behind this curve!
Their runtimes are 87, 95, 104, 117, and 137 minutes.
Compare their density and rug with those for all **797 movies**:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-sparse-runtime-density-reveal
#| fig-cap: Two near identical density charts with widely different numbers of underlying observations.

runtime_reveal_panels = []
for label, values in [('Five movies', sparse_runtimes), ('All movies', runtime_values)]:
    curve = runtime_comparison_curve(label, width=230, height=140)
    ticks = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({'runtime': values}), height=25, width=230).mark_tick(
        opacity=0.4,
    ).encode(
        x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)').scale(domain=[40, 260]),
    )
    runtime_reveal_panels.append(
        (curve & ticks).resolve_scale(x='shared').properties(title=f'{label} (n = {len(values)})')
    )

alt.hconcat(*runtime_reveal_panels)
```

The curves use the same bandwidth and look nearly identical,
but visualizing the individual observations
reveal very different amounts of underlying data.
The smoothness of the curve
comes from the density estimation procedure,
not from having many observations
to support a smooth distribution.
The five-movie curve gives a much
weaker basis for claims about the population's shape,
even though it looks just as convincing.

:::::

::::

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid trusting a density curve just because it looks smooth

Unlike a histogram of counts,
a standard density plot does not tell us
how many observations fall within an interval;
its total area is normalized to one,
whether it represents five movies or five hundred.
A smooth curve is not evidence of a well-supported distribution,
and you should always explore / communicate
how many observations the density chart is constructed from.

:::

Just as for histograms
(but even more important for densities)
the individual observations can be added under the density chart
with a rugplot or siilar.
This can help us see
whether a bump in the density corresponds
to a concentration of observations,
and where a smooth curve extends beyond the observed values.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

We create the density and rug separately, then concatenate them vertically with `&`.
Sharing the x-scale keeps the ticks aligned with their positions on the curve.

```{python}
#| label: runtime-kde-rug-alt
density = alt.Chart(movies, height=200).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    as_=['runtime', 'density'],
    bandwidth=5,
    extent=[40, 260],
).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)'),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q').title('Density'),
)

rug = alt.Chart(movies, height=25).mark_tick(opacity=0.25).encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min:Q').title('Running time (min)'),
)

(density & rug).resolve_scale(x='shared')
```

### ggplot

We add `geom_rug()` to place the individual observations in the margin of the plot.
Transparency helps reveal where many ticks overlap.

```{r}
#| label: runtime-kde-rug-gg
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_density(bw = 5, fill = 'grey80') +
    geom_rug(alpha = 0.25) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(40, 260)) +
    labs(x = 'Running time (min)', y = 'Density')
```

:::

## Multiple distributions

Let's return to comparing the movie genres.
We need a separate density estimate for each genre,
rather than a single estimate for all movies combined.
Using the same bandwidth makes the amount of smoothing comparable between groups.

::: {.callout-warning}

### Avoid hiding distributions behind overlapping areas

Filling under the curves can make their shapes easy to see,
but with several overlapping distributions the filled regions can obscure one another.
Transparency helps, but it does not completely solve the problem.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

Use `groupby` when calculating the densities so that the transform
produces a separate curve for each genre and retains the genre column.
Then map that column to color.
Set `stack(False)` so the areas share a baseline rather than stacking up.

```{python}
#| label: genre-kde-areas-alt
alt.Chart(movies, height=200).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    groupby=['Major Genre'],
    as_=['runtime', 'density'],
    bandwidth=5,
    extent=[40, 260],
).mark_area(opacity=0.5).encode(
    x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)'),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q').title('Density').stack(False),
    color='Major Genre:N',
)
```

### ggplot

Mapping the genre to `fill` also tells ggplot to calculate a density for each group.
Unlike `geom_histogram()`, `geom_density()` does not stack the groups by default.
We add transparency with `alpha`.

```{r}
#| label: genre-kde-areas-gg
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`, fill = `Major Genre`)) +
    geom_density(bw = 5, alpha = 0.5) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(40, 260)) +
    labs(x = 'Running time (min)', y = 'Density')
```

:::

Filled areas can work well when there are only a few distributions
or when they are well separated along the x-axis.
For example, comparing just Comedy and Drama makes the overlap easier to follow:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

```{python}
#| label: two-genre-kde-alt
alt.Chart(
    movies.query('`Major Genre`.isin(["Comedy", "Drama"])'), height=200
).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    groupby=['Major Genre'],
    as_=['runtime', 'density'],
    bandwidth=5,
    extent=[40, 260],
).mark_area(opacity=0.5).encode(
    x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)'),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q').title('Density').stack(False),
    color='Major Genre:N',
)
```

### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: two-genre-kde-gg
ggplot(
    dplyr::filter(movies, `Major Genre` %in% c('Comedy', 'Drama')),
    aes(x = `Running Time min`, fill = `Major Genre`)
) +
    geom_density(bw = 5, alpha = 0.5) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(40, 260)) +
    labs(x = 'Running time (min)', y = 'Density')
```

:::

:::

### Using lines instead of areas

With several distributions in the same chart,
lines can make it easier to follow each curve without hiding the others.
The density calculation stays the same; only the mark changes.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair

```{python}
#| label: genre-kde-lines-alt
alt.Chart(movies, height=200).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    groupby=['Major Genre'],
    as_=['runtime', 'density'],
    bandwidth=5,
    extent=[40, 260],
).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)'),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q').title('Density'),
    color='Major Genre:N',
)
```

#### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: genre-kde-lines-gg
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`, color = `Major Genre`)) +
    geom_density(bw = 5) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(40, 260)) +
    labs(x = 'Running time (min)', y = 'Density')
```

:::

Each group's full density curve has area one,
regardless of how many movies are in that group.
This lets us compare **shapes** without a larger group automatically having a taller curve.
But it also means that a taller peak does not necessarily mean more movies:
it indicates greater concentration relative to the other runtimes within that group.
If the number of observations is central to the question,
show group sizes as well or return to a count-based display.

### Faceting into subplots

Even line plots can become difficult to read when the curves cross repeatedly.
We can separate the genres into facets,
just as we did for histograms.
Putting the facets in a single column aligns their runtime axes,
making differences in location and spread easier to compare.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair

```{python}
#| label: genre-kde-facets-alt
alt.Chart(movies, height=80).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    groupby=['Major Genre'],
    as_=['runtime', 'density'],
    bandwidth=5,
    extent=[40, 260],
).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)'),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q').title('Density'),
).facet(
    'Major Genre:N',
    columns=1,
)
```

#### ggplot

```{r}
#| label: genre-kde-facets-gg
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_density(bw = 5, fill = 'grey80') +
    facet_wrap(vars(`Major Genre`), ncol = 1) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(40, 260)) +
    labs(x = 'Running time (min)', y = 'Density')
```

:::

Now we can compare the broad spread of Adventure runtimes
with the more concentrated Comedy runtimes.
We use common scales so that differences in the curves reflect differences in the data,
rather than a different axis range in each panel.

## Comparing groups with violin plots

A violin plot takes a density curve and mirrors it around a group's position
on a categorical axis.
Its width at a particular runtime shows how concentrated the observations are there.
This gives us a compact way to compare several distributions.

We will use ggplot's violin geom for this representation.
In Altair, we will keep using a column of faceted densities:
these show the same kind of distributional information without mirroring the curves.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair

We can make the facets shorter and omit the density-axis labels
to emphasize comparison along the common runtime axis.
The density scale is still shared between panels.

```{python}
#| label: compact-genre-densities-alt
alt.Chart(movies, height=60).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    groupby=['Major Genre'],
    as_=['runtime', 'density'],
    bandwidth=5,
    extent=[40, 260],
).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)'),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q').title(None).axis(labels=False, ticks=False),
).facet(
    'Major Genre:N',
    columns=1,
)
```

### ggplot

`geom_violin()` calculates the density and draws the mirrored shape.
Because runtime is on the x-axis, these violins lie horizontally.
The `bw` parameter controls smoothing in the same way as for `geom_density()`.

```{r}
#| label: runtime-violins-gg
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`, y = `Major Genre`)) +
    geom_violin(bw = 5, fill = 'grey80') +
    labs(x = 'Running time (min)', y = NULL)
```

By default, violin width does not encode group size.
Setting `scale = 'count'` would make their areas proportional to the number of observations
before trimming, but it changes what their relative sizes mean.

:::

### Adding observations and medians

As with histograms and boxplots,
we can combine the distribution display with the observations it summarizes.
A median provides an additional reference point for comparing the groups.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair

We layer a rug and a dashed median line onto each density,
then facet the combined chart by genre.
The rug makes the observed runtimes visible without giving them a density value.

```{python}
#| label: genre-density-rug-median-alt
density = alt.Chart(movies).transform_density(
    'Running Time min',
    groupby=['Major Genre'],
    as_=['runtime', 'density'],
    bandwidth=5,
    extent=[40, 260],
).mark_area(opacity=0.5).encode(
    x=alt.X('runtime:Q').title('Running time (min)'),
    y=alt.Y('density:Q').title(None),
)

rug = alt.Chart(movies).mark_tick(opacity=0.25, size=8).encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min:Q').title('Running time (min)'),
    y=alt.value(70),
)

median = alt.Chart(movies).mark_rule(color='black', strokeDash=[4, 3]).encode(
    x=alt.X('median(Running Time min):Q').title('Running time (min)'),
)

(density + rug + median).properties(height=70).facet(
    'Major Genre:N',
    columns=1,
)
```

#### ggplot

We add jittered observations and a white point marking the median.
Setting `width = 0` keeps the measured runtimes unchanged;
only positions along the categorical axis are jittered.

```{r}
#| label: runtime-violins-jitter-median-gg
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Movie runtimes by genre. Violins show estimated density, small points show
#|   individual movies, and white points mark the median of each genre.
set.seed(42)
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`, y = `Major Genre`)) +
    geom_violin(bw = 5, fill = 'grey90') +
    geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.1, alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
    geom_point(stat = 'summary', fun = median, shape = 21, fill = 'white', size = 2.5) +
    labs(x = 'Running time (min)', y = NULL)
```

:::

The density and violin displays make the overall shapes easier to compare,
while the observations remind us where the data actually are.
Neither a smooth outline nor a median replaces that information:
they are complementary views of the same distributions.
